papers.title_in_file: Quantum Reservoir Computing for Corrosion Prediction in Aerospace: A Hybrid Approach for Enhanced Material Degradation Forecasting
papers.what_it_is: A short simulation study of an onion-style quantum reservoir computing model that predicts pitting on aluminum alloy samples.

assertions.value: The authors report that their onion quantum reservoir computing model outperforms a simple model and a single classical reservoir for predicting degradation of aluminum alloys, and that adding a classical reservoir layer improves the prediction further.
assertions.anchor: Abstract, p.1; Section V and Fig. 5
quotes: This onion QRC outperforms a simple model and a single classical reservoir for predicting the degradation of aluminum alloys in different environmental conditions.
By combining the onion QRC with an additional classical reservoir layer, the prediction accuracy is further improved.
assertions.certainty_reason: One small-data study; no hardware run stated in the text read.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract claim is stated without numbers; the figures are in Fig. 5 only.

assertions.value: The authors report that the simple averaging model obtains an accuracy of 0.745, that the 3 layer onion QRC tends to do better than the classical reservoir for a range of reservoir sizes, and that 5-layer QRC results improved but not significantly.
quotes: The simple model obtains an accuracy of 0.745.
The 3 layer onion QRC (OQRC) also tends to do better than CRC for a range of classical reservoir sizes.
We also performed calculations for 5-layer QRC and the results were improved but not significantly.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one dataset; the plotted values are in Fig. 5 only.
assertions.reader_inference: The text gives no numeric accuracy for the quantum models, only for the simple baseline.

assertions.value: The authors state that each environment holds 12 samples split into 10 for training and 2 for testing, and that the task is to predict the next 10 days of pitting from the first 3 days using only humidity and temperature.
quotes: Each environment contains 12 samples which we split into 10 for training and 2 for testing.
The prediction problem we will solve is, given the first 3 days of pitting measurements, to predict the next 10 days of corrosion only using the humidity and temperature values
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own dataset and task, Section II, p.2.

assertions.value: The authors acknowledge that each dataset is small.
quotes: Although each dataset is small, part of the promise of QRC is that it is possible to obtain good results
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the size limit of their data, Section II, p.2.
assertions.reader_inference: With 2 test samples per environment, any accuracy difference between models rests on very few samples.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Neural Network applications to protein binding affinity predictions
papers.what_it_is: A simulation study that compares thirty quantum neural network variants with a classical multilayer perceptron for protein binding energy regression.

assertions.value: The authors report that the quantum models were about 20% better in RMSE on the PDBind test set, while the classical baseline was more accurate on the training data and the nanobody set.
quotes: Results indicate that the quantum models achieved approximately 20% higher accuracy on one unseen dataset, although their accuracy was lower on the other datasets.

the baseline NN demonstrated higher accuracy in both the training datasets and the nanobodies dataset. However, the quantum models achieved better accuracy on the PDBind dataset, showing an improvement of approximately 20% in the RMSE metric.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single empirical study with small test sets.
assertions.reader_inference: The result is mixed: better on one of three datasets, worse on two. The 50-sample PDBind set is small.

assertions.value: The authors report that the quantum models trained in times several orders of magnitude shorter than the classical baseline, and attribute this to their much smaller parameter counts.
quotes: Notably, quantum models exhibited training times several orders of magnitude shorter than their classical counterparts
This improvement is likely due to the reduced number of parameters in quantum neural networks, which are orders of magnitude smaller than those of the baseline model.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical timing from one study; the models were simulated.
assertions.reader_inference: The timing compares small simulated circuits with a larger classical network; it does not show a hardware speed advantage.

assertions.value: The authors state that training used 81 protein structure samples, testing used 38 nanobody complexes and 50 PDBind complexes, and that UMAP reduced the original 41 features to 16.
quotes: It consists of 81 protein structure samples with known binding energy values.
decreasing the original 41 features to 16
comprises 38 crystal structure complexes of nanobodies
consists of 50 protein complexes with known binding energy values
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own data setup, Section 3, p.5.

assertions.value: The authors state that finite-shot and noisy simulations are still needed to estimate performance on NISQ hardware.
quotes: Additionally, extending experiments to finite-shot and noisy simulations is essential for realistically estimating performance on NISQ hardware.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors list this as future work, Section 7, p.13.
assertions.reader_inference: The wording implies the reported results come from noiseless simulation.

papers.title_in_file: Improved Financial Forecasting via Quantum Machine Learning
papers.what_it_is: A joint QC Ware and Itau Unibanco study of DPP-enhanced random forests for churn prediction and orthogonal or compound quantum-inspired neural layers for credit risk.

assertions.value: The authors report that, at a fixed recall of 6%, the DPP random forest raised precision from 71.6% for the benchmark model to 77.5%, using classical DPP sampling.
quotes: we optimized hyperparameters and measured the precision for a low fixed recall (6% in this case)
our method showed an improvement in precision from 71.6% for the benchmark model to 77.5% with the new model
assertions.certainty_reason: One bank dataset; the gain was measured with classical DPP sampling, not a quantum computer.
assertions.reader_inference: The reported improvement is a classical result; the quantum circuit was run only on a scaled-down version.

assertions.value: The authors report that the DPP random forest took 54 minutes to train with the best hyperparameters, against 311 seconds for the benchmark model.
quotes: it took 54 minutes to train the model with the best hyperparameters using, compared to 311 seconds for the benchmark model.
assertions.certainty_reason: One timing on one machine.

assertions.value: The authors report that quantum orthogonal and compound layers preserved the performance of fully-connected layers on their credit dataset while using a fraction of the trainable parameters, and that the compound layer showed no advantage over the orthogonal layer.
quotes: The results show that quantum orthogonal and compound layers can preserve the performance of fully-connected layers on this dataset while using a fraction of the trainable parameters.
We note that the ExpResNN did not show advantages over the OrthoResFNN.
assertions.certainty_reason: One dataset; the parameter and Gini figures are in Table 4 only.
assertions.reader_inference: The orthogonal layers train on a classical computer, so the saving is not a quantum advantage.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum hardware is not powerful enough today to give real improvements or conclusive large-scale benchmarks, and report that on an IBM processor the quantum DPP samples gave worse classifier performance as matrix dimensions grew.
quotes: In the present day, quantum hardware is not powerful enough to provide real improvements or conclusive large-scale benchmarks.
However, as the dimensions grow bigger, the samples from the quantum DPP circuits lead to worse classifier performance.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit in Section 8 Conclusion.

papers.title_in_file: Exponential concentration in quantum kernel methods
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper that proves bounds showing quantum kernel values can concentrate exponentially in the qubit number, with numerical checks.

assertions.value: The paper shows that under certain conditions quantum kernel values concentrate exponentially in the number of qubits towards a fixed value, so training with a polynomial number of measurements gives a trivial model whose predictions do not depend on the input.
assertions.anchor: Abstract; Section II Results, Theorems 1 and 3
quotes: We show that, under certain conditions, values of quantum kernels over different input data can be exponentially concentrated (in the number of qubits) towards some fixed value.
Thus on training with a polynomial number of measurements, one ends up with a trivial model where the predictions on unseen inputs are independent of the input data.
assertions.certainty_reason: Analytic bounds derived in Section II (Theorem 1, Theorem 3) and the appendices.

assertions.value: The paper identifies four sources of concentration (expressivity of the data embedding, global measurements, entanglement and noise) and derives a concentration bound for each.
quotes: We identify four sources that can lead to concentration including: expressivity of data embedding, global measurements, entanglement and noise.
For each source, an associated concentration bound of quantum kernels is analytically derived.
assertions.certainty_reason: Bounds derived analytically, Table I and Section II.

assertions.value: The authors state that their noise results show polynomial-depth data embeddings on noisy hardware suffer from exponential concentration, a serious barrier to meaningful quantum advantage in the near term.
quotes: polynomial-depth data embeddings in noisy hardware suffer from exponential concentration, thus presenting a serious barrier to achieve a meaningful quantum advantage in the near-term.
assertions.certainty_reason: Follows from Theorem 3 (noise-induced concentration), Section II.
assertions.reader_inference: The bound applies under the paper's layerwise Pauli noise model, so real devices may differ.

assertions.value: The authors state that their results apply to any method that uses quantum kernels, and that the results should not be read as condemning quantum kernel methods but as a prompt to develop embeddings free of concentration.
quotes: Our results apply generally to any method that involves quantum kernels.
we stress our results should not be understood as condemning quantum kernel methods
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state their own scope, Section II.A and Section III.

papers.title_in_file: Supervised Quantum Machine Learning: A Future Outlook from Qubits to Enterprise Applications
papers.what_it_is: A short review of supervised quantum machine learning with a ten-year outlook.

assertions.value: The authors state that as of 2025 practical demonstrations of quantum advantage in supervised learning remain limited, and that a reproducible advantage on real-world tasks has not yet been shown.
quotes: As of 2025, practical demonstrations of quantum advantage in supervised learning remain limited
a reproducible advantage over classical methods on real-world tasks has yet to be empirically demonstrated
assertions.certainty_reason: A review statement that cites other work; no new experiment.

assertions.value: The authors report, citing an IonQ study, a text classification task on a trapped-ion computer with over 10,000 data points and an average accuracy of 62% on a five-way task.
quotes: The experiment involved classifying over 10,000 textual data points in a natural language processing (NLP) context.
The researchers achieved an average accuracy of 62% on a five-way classification task
assertions.certainty_reason: Result attributed to another study (reference 28 in the paper).

assertions.value: The authors cite Anschuetz and Kiani as showing that many shallow variational circuits can be untrainable even without barren plateaus because of poor optimization landscapes.
quotes: Anschuetz and Kiani [29] demonstrated that, even in the absence of barren plateaus, many shallow variational circuits can be untrainable due to the presence of poor optimization landscapes, including numerous local minima.
assertions.certainty_reason: Result attributed to another paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that until large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computers are available, meaningful QML applications will likely stay limited to shallow circuits on small-scale datasets.
quotes: Until large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computers become available, meaningful QML applications will likely remain constrained to shallow circuits on small-scale datasets.
assertions.certainty_reason: Author outlook, no evidence in the paper.

papers.what_it_is: A simulation study of Bayesian optimization as the classical optimizer for QAOA on Max-Cut and Max Independent Set.

assertions.value: The authors report that on a Max-Cut graph Bayesian optimization stops at a lower approximation ratio than basin-hopping and dual annealing but reaches the target ratio with far fewer circuit runs, as the other two methods take, in order, 1400 and 10800.
quotes: We see that Bayesian optimization stops at a lower R than basin-hopping and dual annealing
compared to the other two methods which take, in order, 1400 and 10800.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation on one graph; the Bayesian run count is in the same sentence as a symbol that did not extract.
assertions.reader_inference: Only two graphs were tested, so the generality of the saving is not established.

assertions.value: The authors report that using 1024 measurements instead of the exact energy lowers the approximation ratio by 5%, and that in Section IV 128 shots reduce it by 5% relative to 1024 shots.
quotes: We have showed that the results are slightly altered by a 5% decrease in the approximation ratio by using 1024 measurements compared to the optimization with the exact energy.
we see that taking NS = 128 shots reduces R by 5% w.r.t. NS = 1024
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation result.
assertions.reader_inference: The two statements compare different shot counts against different references, so the paper's own wording is inconsistent.

assertions.value: The authors report that in simulation the method is robust to noise at low circuit depths, while for deeper circuits noise intensity noticeably affects the final approximation ratio.
quotes: we find that for low circuit depths it is robust against noise.
intensity of noise sensibly affects the final approximation ratio, as expected.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulated noise model, not hardware.

assertions.value: The authors state that results are obtained on two 3-regular graphs of 6 and 10 nodes, and that noise is simulated by adding random noise to every QAOA parameter.
quotes: The following results are obtained on two 3-regular graphs of 6 and 10 nodes
we add random noise on every QAOA parameter
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own test graphs and noise model, Section IV.

papers.title_in_file: Analog QAOA with Bayesian Optimisation on a neutral atom QPU
papers.what_it_is: A study of analog QAOA with Bayesian optimisation for Maximum Independent Set, with simulations and runs on Pasqal's Orion Alpha neutral atom processor.

assertions.value: The authors report that a closed-loop optimisation on a 15-qubit graph at depth 5 succeeded on the QPU, with the solution bitstring measured more often than any other.
quotes: Finally, we run one optimisation loop on a N = 15 qubits graph (inset of Fig. 4 with the MIS solution highlighted in red) with depth p = 5.
The experimental optimisation was successful: in Fig. 4 we show the final state with the solution bitstring measured more often than all the other ones.
assertions.certainty_reason: One hardware run on one graph.
assertions.reader_inference: One graph of 15 atoms is a proof of feasibility, not a scaling result. A coauthor is from Pasqal, the device maker.

assertions.value: The authors report that for the 11-qubit instance optimisation was rather successful, but the approximation ratio and fidelity results show more shots seem to be needed for a reliable optimisation.
quotes: Although optimisation is rather successful also for N = 11 (final Sr tells us that the solution state stands out), the R and F results show that for this instance, more shots seem to be needed for a more reliable optimisation.
assertions.certainty_reason: One hardware run.

assertions.value: The authors report that in simulation, reducing the number of shots does not necessarily compromise optimisation results and may even give better outcomes in some cases.
quotes: This suggests that reducing the number of shots does not necessarily compromise optimisation results, and may even yield better outcomes in certain cases.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation at one small system size.

assertions.value: The authors state that larger graphs need a larger p, giving longer sequences and more quantum error, and that more work is needed to confirm efficiency on larger systems and more complex problem classes.
quotes: an identified limitation of the QAOA approach is the need for increased p to further improve a score, leading to longer sequences
more work is needed to confirm the efficiency of the method to larger systems and more complex problem classes
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state these limits in the Conclusion and outlook.

papers.title_in_file: An Efficient Quantum Classifier Based on Hamiltonian Representations
papers.what_it_is: A simulation study of a Hamiltonian classifier that encodes data as an observable, tested on text and image classification.

assertions.value: The authors report that the Hamiltonian classifier delivers performance comparable to or better than established classical and quantum baselines on text and image classification.
quotes: The Hamiltonian classifier delivers performance comparable to or better than these methods.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulated benchmark on several datasets; per-dataset accuracies are in Tables 2 and 3.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper separately says its results do not match state-of-the-art NLP models.

assertions.value: The authors claim an encoding with logarithmic qubit and gate complexity relative to input dimensionality, and note that total gate complexity depends entirely on the chosen circuit.
quotes: achieves a favourable logarithmic qubit and gate complexity relative to the input dimensionality
gate complexity depends entirely on the chosen circuit U
assertions.certainty_reason: Scaling argument by the authors; Table 1 lists the orders.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract says logarithmic in gates, but the body ties total gate count to the variational circuit chosen.

assertions.value: The authors state that the classifier is presently a proof of concept and that noisy simulations and real hardware are outside the scope of the work.
quotes: The Hamiltonian classifier is presently a proof of concept meant to illustrate a novel input scheme for quantum devices
Noisy simulations and real hardware implementation fall outside the scope of this work, as the current model was not designed with noise resilience in mind.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state these limits in Section 5 and Limitations.

assertions.value: The authors state that theory on flipped models suggests a definitive advantage needs more advanced devices, so it is unrealistic to expect these models to surpass classical counterparts at this stage.
quotes: making it unrealistic to expect these models to surpass classical counterparts at this stage.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this in the Limitations section.
